title: 2017 Pymble Legal Studies Trial
notes: Scanned paper read from rendered pages. No answer key is included.

groups.stimulus: 19-year-old Ben, who is unknown to police, is given a ‘move along’ order. He refuses, abuses the police, then struggles and hits one officer with his cap as they try to arrest him.

questions.stem: The international Covenant on Civil and Political Rights can best be described as which of the following?
questions.answerNote: ICCPR is a treaty (1966) ratified by Australia.

questions.stem: With which offence could Ben be charged?
questions.answerNote: Ben struggles with and strikes an officer: resist/hinder arrest and assault police. B (public order) is weaker as the stem stresses the struggle and hit.

questions.stem: Assuming that Ben pleads not guilty, in which court will Ben’s hearing take place?
questions.answerNote: Assault police/resist arrest are summary (Table 1) offences, heard in the Local Court; Ben is 19, so not the Children's Court.

questions.stem: Alice has received an official legal document in relation to an offence she has allegedly committed. She is required to attend the local court on a certain date. What is the legal document known as?
questions.answerNote: A Court Attendance Notice requires attendance at Local Court.

questions.stem: When denying a bail application, which of the following would be a determining factor?
questions.answerNote: Seriousness/number of victims weighs against bail; The other options favour bail.

questions.stem: The United Nations Human Rights Council is an example of which of the following?
questions.answerNote: UN Human Rights Council is an intergovernmental body of member states.

questions.stem: What is the role of the International Criminal Court?

options.A: To enforce the rule of law
options.C: To prosecute crimes against the international community.

questions.answerNote: ICC prosecutes genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, aggression.

questions.stem: Jake has planned to commit a robbery. However, he is unable to execute his plan due to illness. This is an example of which of the following?
questions.answerNote: Planning without executing is a preliminary offence (attempt/conspiracy/incitement).

questions.stem: Marilyn has been arrested and detained by police. In order to ensure that any information provided by Marilyn, during questioning, is admissible in court, what must the police do?

options.B: Caution her as to her rights
options.D: Keep a written record of everything she says

questions.answerNote: Under LEPRA, police must caution the detained person before questioning for admissibility.

questions.stem: A jury has been deliberating for two days and has informed the judge that they are unable to reach a verdict. What can the judge do?

options.D: Allow a majority verdict with one dissenter

questions.answerNote: Under Jury Act s55F a majority verdict of 11:1 is allowed after at least 8 hours of deliberation. C is looser but D is more exact.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the primary purpose of the United Nations?

options.A: To develop friendly relations among nations
options.B: To develop treaties that relate to human rights
options.C: To reprimand nations who breach human rights
options.D: To prosecute those who have breached international law

questions.answerNote: UN Charter art 1: primary purpose is to maintain international peace and security; Of the options, developing friendly relations is the stated purpose.

questions.stem: Having committed a summary offence, 14-year-old Matthew has been convicted by a Children’s Court Magistrate. Which penalty is he most likely to receive?
questions.answerNote: Children's Court sentencing for a summary offence is likely a good behaviour bond/ non-custodial; 12 months prison unlikely and ICO not available to children.

questions.stem: A judge grants a defendant’s request for a criminal trial without a jury. Which term best describes what has been achieved for the defendant?
questions.answerNote: Judge-alone trial responds to the individual circumstances (e.g. Prejudicial publicity), which is fairness, not equality.

questions.stem: What effect does the separation of powers have on human rights in Australia?

options.A: The High Court is able to amend legislation.
options.B: The judiciary is able to interpret legislation.
options.C: The executive can change judicial decisions.
options.D: The Governor-General can review High Court decisions.

questions.answerNote: Separation of powers: judiciary interprets/applies law, does not make it.

questions.stem: Lisa, an Australian citizen, has been charged with importing $4 million of drugs from Singapore into Sydney. In which court will her case be heard?
questions.answerNote: Of the options, only NSW Supreme Court is a possible trial court (federal drug import offence tried in state courts; Usually District/Supreme). Drug Court is for drug-dependent offenders, ICC no jurisdiction, Singapore irrelevant.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of preventative detention?

options.C: To protect the victim of crime
options.D: To balance the rights of offenders and society

questions.answerNote: Preventative detention is about protecting the community from a person assessed as dangerous.

questions.stem: An incarcerated person is granted day-release into the community. This is an example of which of the following?

options.D: An exercise of the judge’s discretion

questions.answerNote: Day release is a decision after sentencing (corrections/parole authority), not bail or judicial discretion.

questions.stem: Gareth, a 15-year old, has been charged with a serious criminal offence. Which of the following statements is true?

options.B: Gareth will be treated as an adult in court.
options.C: There is a rebuttable presumption of doli incapax.
options.D: The presumption of doli incapax is not relevant in this case.

questions.answerNote: The presumption applies only to ages 10-14; 15-year-old is outside it. C is a tempting distractor but is irrelevant to Gareth.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the impact of state sovereignty on the effectiveness of international laws?

options.A: Significant, as countries must observe international laws
options.B: Significant, as countries can choose to ignore international laws
options.C: Limited, as the international community works closely together
options.D: Limited, as many countries retain legal control of their parliament

questions.answerNote: State sovereignty means countries can choose to ignore international law, which limits its effectiveness; B and D are both plausible but D's reasoning (control of parliament) is less direct. B is preferred.

questions.stem: In sentencing Peter for an indictable offence, the judge wants the penalty to reflect the serious nature of the offence without imprisoning him. Which of the following options is most likely?
questions.answerNote: Indictable offence, serious but non-custodial: community service (a CCO with community service work) fits best; Diversionary programs are for minor offences; Probation order is no longer a NSW sentence.
